newsitem.title: TANZANIA: IMF asks Tanzania's Mkapa to oppose tax holidays.
newsitem.headline: IMF asks Tanzania's Mkapa to oppose tax holidays.

text.p: IMF officials have asked Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa to oppose the granting of tax holidays as an incentive to boost investment and local business confidence, diplomatic and financial sources said on Friday.

Mkapa's intervention was sought after a meeting on Tuesday with senior officials of the International Monetary Fund. The IMF team was led by Washington-based assistant director for fiscal affairs, Jeffrey Davis.
The IMF is concerned about the inclusion of tax holidays in a draft bill called the Tanzania Investment Incentive Act, due to be debated in parliament in April.
"The hope is this act won't see the light of day for a while. It's loaded with too many giveaways," said one IMF official who asked not to be named.
Financial sources said proposals being contemplated by Tanzania included tax holidays of between five to 15 years for new investments over $300,000.
But the IMF was concerned that the bill in its present form contained too many "giveaways" and could undermine hard-won improvements to Tanzania's budgetary performance.

Economic reforms from the 1980s have improved Tanzania's fortunes. The currency is now stable, reserves are up and annual inflation in January was 14 percent from 25 percent a year ago, according to government figures.

Government revenues in January totalled 45 billion shillings ($75 million), 12 billion shillings higher than for the same period a year ago. Revenues from July 1996 to January 1997 totalled 331.1 billion shillings or 58 percent of the budget estimate for 1996/97.
In talks described as "very sensitive" the IMF team asked Mkapa, in the words of one official: "not to knuckle under to pressure from the business community."
IMF concern about tax holidays received the support of the local British business lobby and the East Africa Association (EAA) which has influential business links to the region.
EAA chief executive Chris Buckmaster said with the exception of the mining industry, he opposed random granting of tax holidays as an incentive to boost foreign investment.
He suggested the Tanzanian government implement a low tax regime with generous allowances and as low a corporate tax base as possible.

A complicated and outdated taxation system coupled with choking bureacracy are seen as two major impediments to foreign investment in Tanzania. The government has promised action on tax reform but international lending institutions have warned against "quick fix" remedies.
